rewrites.summary:
Delhi sits at the centre of the country's 2026 reversal on trans rights: parliament passed an amendment bill removing the right to self-identification, restricting legal recognition to traditionally accepted socio-cultural groups and intersex people, mandating medical certification, and creating new offences of coercion and allurement punishable up to life imprisonment — a de facto reversal of the 2014 constitutional self-determination ruling, cleared by both houses and awaiting presidential assent. The bill triggered rallies in the capital in March 2026, and a supreme-court-appointed advisory panel urged its withdrawal amid privacy and dignity challenges.

The capital is also where the country's trans population is most institutionally visible: the most recent national census recorded 487,803 transgender persons, of whom roughly 32,500 held identity documents — the documentation gap and the protest politics both concentrate here.

rewrites.summary:
The capital's courts have been the country's clearest rights forum for trans people: a ruling finalised in July 2024 held that police who told a transgender person mid-legal-transition to avoid public restrooms for a while had infringed personal rights, calling comfortable restroom use a fundamental and universal human right and awarding damages. A 2021 national human-rights-commission survey (591 trans respondents) quantified the underlying fear: 41% had used a restroom of another gender out of fear of mistreatment, 39% restricted food and drink to avoid public restrooms, 36% went without; a 2021 district-court judgment awarded damages against a beauty academy that barred a trans student's restroom use.

Recognition has also liberalised judicially: a May 2024 regional decision approved gender-marker change for five trans people without surgery, holding that a surgery requirement violates bodily integrity and reducing the old surgical prerequisites to reference-only status, though some courts still apply them.

A 2021 lower-court damages award against an academy that barred a trans student, and a May 2024 regional precedent allowing marker change without surgery (surgical prerequisites demoted to reference-only), complete the judicial picture.

rewrites.summary:
This state is where the country's religious-enforcement apparatus has been most visibly exercised against gender expression: in 2021 its religious department issued an arrest warrant for a prominent transgender businesswoman over her presentation and mobilised 122 religious-affairs officers in a manhunt that preceded her leaving the country, an episode documented in international analysis of state-backed discrimination against LGBT people in Malaysia.

The national framework applies unchanged here: same-sex conduct is criminalised with sentences up to 20 years and whipping, there is no legal gender recognition, and the day-to-day exposure for gender-nonconforming visitors runs precisely through this state's religious-offence enforcement.

rewrites.summary:
Lima concentrates the country's sharpest documented lethality and its newest legal restriction. An LGBTI human-rights observatory at a national university counted 54 LGBTI+ murders for 2020–2023, with trans women the most affected, amid rising hate crimes. In 2025 the national congress — sitting and operating out of the capital — approved a norm against trans people's use of public bathrooms (committee vote February 2025; floor vote April 2025), which a national human-rights institute published an analysis calling legalised discrimination with direct consequences for access to public space.

For a trans visitor, the capital is therefore where both mechanisms bite: the bathroom-restriction norm is national policy administered here, and the murder pattern shows the violence risk when prosecutions are rare and official statistics thin.

Enforcement of both the violence pattern and the norm concentrates in this jurisdiction.

rewrites.summary:
Ankara is the administrative core of what the country's leading LGBTI rights organisation — reporting from its capital launch event in 2025 — documented as hostility turned into explicit state policy: presidency-centred targeting, the family ministry as implementing body, broadcast and platform censorship, an LGBTI organisation closed, six violations of the right to life (three recorded as hate-motivated) with trans people most affected, and no official hate-crime statistics in existence. A leaked October 2025 judicial package would add up to three years' imprisonment for conduct contrary to biological sex and its promotion, and bar gender-affirming care below age 25.

The capital hosts the machinery that drafts and enforces those measures; nothing on record shows local countervailing protection, and the same courts and ministries that field the report operate here.

Enforcement architecture is concentrated in this city; no local protection is documented.

rewrites.summary:
Gaziantep sits fully under the national framework with no documented local divergence in either direction: the leaked October 2025 judicial package would criminalise conduct contrary to biological sex and its promotion (up to three years) and restrict gender-affirming care to age 25 and above, while the 2025 national rights report documents hostility as explicit state policy — presidency-centred targeting, censorship, an organisation closed, six violations of the right to life with trans people most affected, and no official protection statistics at all.

Nothing in the record shows this province offering either special danger beyond, or protection beneath, that national baseline; a visibly trans visitor's exposure is the national one, locally enforced.

No provincial-specific protection or aggravation is documented; exposure follows the national pattern.
